blocks.content: Every other topic in this module handed you one tool at a time. How to ask clarifying questions. How to run the back of the envelope math. How to spot the part of a design that breaks first. How to defend a trade off out loud. Useful on their own, but an actual interview never hands you the tools one at a time. It hands you 45 minutes and a single vague sentence, and expects you to reach for every tool, in order, without anyone telling you which one comes next.

This lesson is the rehearsal for that. We are going to pick one prompt, a URL shortener, and walk it start to finish exactly the way a real interview would unfold. Not a checklist of things a URL shortener needs. A continuous thirty minute conversation, compressed onto the page, where every section is a phase you already learned about elsewhere in this module and are now watching in motion.

blocks.title: Why a URL shortener
blocks.content: It sounds almost too simple for a capstone, but that is exactly the point. It is small enough that we can actually finish it in one lesson, yet it has a real core design decision buried in it, how do you generate the short code, and a real bottleneck once it scales, which makes it a genuinely good stand in for harder prompts like a chat app or a ride hailing service.
1. Introduction

Think of this the way a pilot thinks of a full flight simulation after weeks of studying individual instruments. You already know what the altimeter does and what the throttle does. The simulation is where you find out if you can fly the whole plane, instrument by instrument, in the right order, under time pressure. That is what this walkthrough is.

We are going to treat the interviewer as a real person sitting across from you, asking one line: design a URL shortener. Everything after that line is us, the candidate, driving the conversation forward one phase at a time.
1.1 What this walkthrough covers

blocks.content: 1.2 The prompt we are using
Design a URL shortener, something like a service where a user pastes a long link and gets back a short one that redirects to it.

That is the entire prompt. No scale mentioned. No mention of analytics, custom aliases, or expiration. That vagueness is not an oversight on the interviewer's part, it is the whole test. What you do in the next two minutes matters more than anything you draw for the rest of the interview.
2. Clarifying the Requirements

blocks.title: Interview phase: requirement clarification
blocks.content: This is the phase covered in depth in the requirement clarification topic elsewhere in this module. Here we are just running it live, on this specific prompt, so you can see it actually happen instead of reading about it in the abstract.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384088-828182136.png
blocks.alt: The clarification dialogue outcome, moving from the vague prompt through a few pointed questions to a locked in set of assumptions

blocks.content: A candidate who skips this and jumps straight to drawing boxes is making a bet, that the interviewer's unstated version of a URL shortener matches whatever version happens to be in the candidate's head. That is a bad bet. Two minutes of questions here saves you from redesigning something at minute thirty because you assumed wrong.
2.1 The questions worth asking

["What scale are we talking about, are we talking about a small internal tool or something like bit dot ly serving the whole internet","Do users need to pick their own custom alias, or is a randomly generated short code enough","Do links expire, or do they live forever once created","Do we need click analytics, like a count of how many times a link was used","Is this read heavy, meaning far more people clicking links than people creating them"]
items: What scale are we talking about, are we talking about a small internal tool or something like bit dot ly serving the whole internet
Do users need to pick their own custom alias, or is a randomly generated short code enough
Do links expire, or do they live forever once created
Do we need click analytics, like a count of how many times a link was used
Is this read heavy, meaning far more people clicking links than people creating them

blocks.content: Notice that none of these questions are about the database or the algorithm yet. They are all about scope. You are not designing anything until you know what you are designing.
2.2 The assumptions we land on

Say the interviewer answers roughly like this. Assume a service used broadly, similar in spirit to a public shortener. No custom aliases for now, we can mention them as a later extension. Links do not expire by default, but a user can optionally set an expiry date. Basic click count analytics would be nice to have. And yes, it is heavily read dominant, most links get created once and clicked many times over their life.

{"headers":["Assumption","What it means for the design"],"rows":[["Public scale service","We size the system for millions of daily users, not a small internal tool"],["No custom aliases in v1","The ID generator only needs to produce codes, not validate arbitrary user text"],["Optional expiry","The schema needs an expiry field and something that periodically enforces it"],["Nice to have analytics","A lightweight, asynchronous pipeline is enough, it should never sit on the critical redirect path"],["Read heavy","Caching is going to matter a lot more than write throughput"]]}

blocks.title: Say your assumptions out loud
blocks.content: Even when the interviewer does not push back, state the assumption anyway. It gives them a chance to correct you early, and it shows you are designing on purpose rather than by accident.
3. Capacity Estimation

blocks.title: Interview phase: capacity estimation
blocks.content: This is the phase the capacity estimation topic covers in depth. The goal is never a perfectly accurate number, it is a rough sense of scale that tells you whether you need one server or a fleet of them, and whether a single database will hold up.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384088-36073951.png
blocks.alt: Capacity numbers flowing from daily active users through new links created per day to total redirects per day and peak read QPS

blocks.content: Let us put real numbers on the assumptions from the last section. Assume 10 million daily active users. Only a small fraction of them actually shorten a new link on a given day, most people are just clicking links other people made. Say 1 million new short links get created per day.
3.1 Traffic, from DAU to QPS

Write traffic first. 1 million new links a day, spread across 86400 seconds in a day, comes out to roughly 12 writes per second on average. Traffic is never flat though, so plan for a peak multiplier of around three times, which puts peak write throughput at roughly 35 requests per second. That is a small number, almost any reasonably provisioned API layer handles that without breaking a sweat.

Read traffic is the more interesting number, because this system is read heavy by our own assumption. A reasonable read to write ratio for a link shortener is around 100 to 1, since each link tends to get clicked far more times than it gets created. That puts redirects at roughly 100 million a day. Divide by 86400 seconds and you land at roughly 1160 reads per second on average, and with the same three times peak multiplier, somewhere around 3500 reads per second at peak.
{"headers":["Metric","Average","Peak, roughly three times average"],"rows":[["Writes per second, new links","12","35"],["Reads per second, redirects","1160","3500"]]}

blocks.title: The exact multiplier does not matter
blocks.content: Whether you use two times or three times or five times for peak traffic will not make or break the interview. What matters is that you explicitly account for the fact that traffic is not flat, and that you can defend whatever number you picked if asked.
3.2 Storage, and how fast it grows
blocks.text: 3.2 Storage, and how fast it grows

blocks.content: Each stored record needs a short code, the original long URL, and a bit of metadata like a creation timestamp, an optional expiry date, and a click counter. A generous estimate puts that at around 500 bytes per record once you include index overhead.

At 1 million new records a day, that is roughly 500 megabytes of new data every day. Over a year that is a bit under 200 gigabytes, and over five years you are looking at just under a terabyte total. That is a big number in absolute terms, but it is entirely manageable for a modern database, especially since old, rarely clicked links can eventually be moved to cheaper cold storage.

One more useful number while we are here, how many unique codes we actually need. If a short code is 7 characters long using a base62 alphabet, lowercase letters, uppercase letters, and digits, that gives 62 to the power of 7, which is a little over three and a half trillion possible codes. At 1 million new codes a day that space would take us over nine thousand years to exhaust. Seven characters is comfortably enough.
4. High Level Architecture

blocks.title: Interview phase: high level architecture
blocks.content: This is where you actually put boxes on the board. Notice how little time we spent getting here, two short sections, because the clarification and the estimation up front made this part almost mechanical.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384088-85296009.png
blocks.alt: A high level sketch of the client talking to an API layer, which fans out to an ID generator, a cache, and a database

blocks.content: At this scale the building blocks are refreshingly simple. A client, a stateless API layer that can be horizontally scaled behind a load balancer, an ID generator for producing short codes, a database that holds the mapping from short code to long URL, and a cache sitting in front of that database for the read path.
4.1 The building blocks, one line each
blocks.text: 4.1 The building blocks, one line each

blocks.content: ["Client, a browser or app that either submits a long URL or clicks an existing short link","API layer, stateless servers handling both the create request and the redirect request, easy to scale horizontally since there is no session state to worry about","ID generator, the component responsible for producing a unique short code for every new long URL, more on this in the next section","Database, the source of truth mapping a short code to its original long URL plus metadata","Cache, sits in front of the database on the read path so popular links do not have to hit disk on every single click"]
items: Client, a browser or app that either submits a long URL or clicks an existing short link
API layer, stateless servers handling both the create request and the redirect request, easy to scale horizontally since there is no session state to worry about
ID generator, the component responsible for producing a unique short code for every new long URL, more on this in the next section
Database, the source of truth mapping a short code to its original long URL plus metadata
Cache, sits in front of the database on the read path so popular links do not have to hit disk on every single click

blocks.content: 4.2 The write path, shortening a URL
blocks.text: 4.2 The write path, shortening a URL

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384664-111678720.png
blocks.alt: The write path, a client submitting a long URL through the API layer to the ID generator and then into the database

blocks.content: A user pastes a long URL and hits submit. The API layer receives it, asks the ID generator for a fresh short code, and writes a new row into the database mapping that code to the long URL, along with the creation time and optional expiry. The API layer then returns the short link to the user. Writes are infrequent enough, only 12 a second on average by our earlier math, that this path rarely needs much special handling.
4.3 The read path, following a short link
blocks.text: 4.3 The read path, following a short link

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384666-986228819.png
blocks.alt: The read path, a client opening a short link through the API layer, a cache lookup, and a fallback to the database on a miss

blocks.content: A user clicks a short link. The API layer looks up the code, checks the cache first, and if it is there, immediately issues a redirect. If it is not in the cache, it falls back to the database, fetches the long URL, writes it into the cache for next time, and then redirects. This is the path that carries essentially all of the system's load, which is exactly why the next section spends so much time on it.
5. The Core Design Decision, Generating Short Codes
blocks.text: 5. The Core Design Decision, Generating Short Codes

blocks.title: Interview phase: deep dive and tradeoff justification
blocks.content: Every interview has one component worth spending real time on instead of skimming past. In this design, it is this one. This is also where the trade off justification topic in this module gets exercised the most directly.

There are three broad ways to produce a short code for a long URL, and each one makes a different promise and a different sacrifice. Walking an interviewer through all three, out loud, and picking one with a reason, is worth more than silently drawing whichever one you happen to remember.
5.1 Option one, counter based
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384667-29772032.png
blocks.alt: Counter based generation, a global counter producing the next integer value, which gets base62 encoded into a short code

blocks.content: Keep a single, ever increasing counter. Every time a new URL comes in, take the next integer, encode it in base62, and that is your short code. It is simple, it is guaranteed unique by construction, and it never needs a collision check.

The catch is that a single global counter becomes a coordination point. Every write needs to agree on the next value, which is fine at 12 writes a second, but becomes an actual bottleneck if this design ever needs to scale writes by a hundred times. It is also mildly predictable, since codes increase in a guessable order, which is a minor concern if you do not want people enumerating your links.
5.2 Option two, hash based
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384668-722371133.png
blocks.alt: Hash based generation, hashing the long URL, taking the first several characters, checking for a collision, and retrying with a salt if needed

blocks.content: Take the long URL, run it through a hash function like MD5 or SHA256, and take the first 7 characters of the resulting hash as your short code. This avoids any single coordination point entirely, since any server can compute a hash independently without talking to anything else.

The catch here is collisions. Truncating a hash to 7 characters means two different long URLs can, occasionally, produce the same short code. You have to check the database for that code before committing, and if it is taken, retry with a small salt appended to the input and hash again. Rare, but it happens, and the design has to account for it explicitly rather than pretend it cannot.
5.3 Option three, random with a collision retry
blocks.text: 5.3 Option three, random with a collision retry

blocks.content: Generate 7 random base62 characters directly, no hashing involved, then check if that code already exists in the database. If it does, generate another one and check again. This is the simplest of the three to reason about and it avoids the predictability problem of the counter approach entirely, since there is no pattern to the codes at all.

The trade off is the same collision retry cost as the hash approach, plus the fact that every single write now needs at least one database lookup before it can even attempt the insert. At our actual write volume of 12 a second that lookup is cheap, but it is worth naming as the cost you are accepting.
5.4 What we would actually say in the interview
blocks.text: 5.4 What we would actually say in the interview

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Counter based: no collisions possible, trivial to reason about","Counter based: a single coordination point, mildly predictable codes"],["Hash based: no central coordination, any server computes it alone","Hash based: needs a collision check and a retry path"],["Random with retry: unpredictable, simple logic","Random with retry: a database lookup on every single write"]]}

Given our numbers, 12 writes a second on average and 35 at peak, the honest answer is that all three options would work fine at this scale. The interesting part of the answer is not which one is objectively best, it is that you can reason about when each one stops working. If write volume grew a hundred times, the counter approach's single coordination point would become the first thing to fix, likely by handing out counter ranges to each server in blocks instead of a single shared counter. That single sentence, said out loud, tends to matter more to an interviewer than picking the correct answer, because there usually is not one.

For this walkthrough, say we pick the hash based approach, since it avoids any central coordination and keeps every API server fully independent. Here is roughly what the encoding step looks like in code.

blocks.title: Say the collision odds out loud
blocks.content: With 7 base62 characters that is over three and a half trillion possible codes, so at 1 million new links a day, the odds of hitting a collision on any given insert are extremely small. Naming that number out loud shows the interviewer you are not just retrying blindly, you understand why the retry loop almost never actually runs.
6. The First Bottleneck, and Fixing It
blocks.text: 6. The First Bottleneck, and Fixing It

blocks.title: Interview phase: bottleneck identification
blocks.content: This is the moment in the interview where you stop describing what your design does and start describing what breaks it. That shift is exactly what the bottleneck identification topic trains on its own, we are just applying it here.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384668-741414429.png
blocks.alt: The first bottleneck, database reads spiking as traffic grows, fixed by adding a caching layer that absorbs most of the load

blocks.content: Go back to the numbers from section 3. Reads outnumber writes roughly 100 to 1, and peak read traffic sits around 3500 requests per second. If every single one of those redirects hit the database directly, that database would be doing almost nothing but serving the same small set of popular links over and over, which is a waste of an expensive resource on completely repetitive work.
6.1 Where the system actually breaks first
blocks.text: 6.1 Where the system actually breaks first

blocks.content: This is the read path we sketched back in section 4.3. As daily active users grow past our estimate, redirect traffic grows with them, and the database's read capacity becomes the ceiling on the whole system, well before the write side or the API layer ever becomes a concern. Link popularity also tends to follow a power law, a small number of links get the overwhelming majority of clicks, think of a link shared in a viral post versus a random one off share in a private chat.
6.2 Fixing it with a cache in front of the database
blocks.text: 6.2 Fixing it with a cache in front of the database

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384669-239149597.png
blocks.alt: A redirect request hitting the cache first, returning instantly on a hit, and only falling through to the database on a miss

blocks.content: Put a cache, something like Redis, in front of the database on the read path exactly as sketched earlier. Because link popularity is so skewed, a relatively small cache can absorb the overwhelming majority of read traffic. If the top 20 percent of links account for 80 percent of clicks, caching just that hot set turns most of your 3500 peak reads per second into cache hits that never touch the database at all.

This also naturally reduces load on the database enough that it can keep serving writes and the rarer cold link lookups without contention. The trade off worth naming is cache staleness, if a link's destination or expiry status changes, the cache needs to be invalidated, or you set a modest time to live on cache entries and accept a small window of staleness in exchange for simplicity.
7. Non Functional Considerations

blocks.title: Interview phase: wrap up and non functional considerations
blocks.content: These usually come up in the last five minutes of a real interview. You will not go as deep here as on the core design decision, and that is fine, the goal is to show you have not forgotten they exist.
7.1 Availability

The API layer is stateless, so it scales horizontally behind a load balancer without any special handling, if one instance dies, the load balancer simply stops sending it traffic. The database is the part that actually needs deliberate redundancy, a primary with one or more replicas, so a failure does not take the whole read path down with it. Since this system is read heavy, replicas also double as extra read capacity even outside of a failure scenario.
7.2 Analytics

We agreed earlier that basic click analytics would be nice to have, but explicitly not required on the critical path. The right shape for this is asynchronous, when a redirect happens, fire off a lightweight event to a queue instead of incrementing a counter synchronously inside the same request. A separate consumer processes those events and updates click counts in its own time. This keeps the redirect itself fast no matter how busy the analytics pipeline gets.
7.3 Expiring links
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384669-324420312.png
blocks.alt: The lifecycle of an expiring link, from creation with a TTL attached through a background scan to removal and a 404 on future clicks

blocks.content: Since a user can optionally set an expiry date, store that expiry alongside the mapping and check it on every read before honoring a redirect. A background job can also periodically sweep expired links out of both the database and the cache, so storage does not grow forever with dead links nobody will ever click again. Until that sweep runs, a simple check at read time is enough to make sure nobody gets redirected somewhere the link owner intended to shut off.
